risk_rationale: Headline CPI re-accelerated 49bp to 3.8% YoY while Core PCE sits at 3.2%, well above the Fed's 2% target, eliminating near-term rate cut optionality. WTI at $109.8 and Brent at $118.3 introduce a persistent energy-driven inflation tail risk. Simultaneous softening in labor demand (NFP 115K, U-3 4.3%) points to stagflationary pressure that limits the Fed's policy flexibility.
outlook_headline: Stagflationary dynamics are reasserting — sticky inflation with decelerating growth and a labor market losing momentum is the worst combination for risk assets.
outlook_body: Real GDP at 2.0% annualized provides only a thin cushion against a further growth deceleration, and the consumer is visibly stressed: the personal saving rate has compressed to 3.6% while credit card delinquencies have climbed to 2.9%. The CPI re-acceleration to 3.8% — led in part by energy with WTI at $109.8 — closes the door on Fed easing and raises the probability of a prolonged hold or a hawkish policy pivot. Housing remains under structural pressure with the 30Y mortgage at 6.37%, even as starts held at 1,502K, suggesting supply is not the binding constraint. Portfolio positioning should lean defensive across duration and credit until inflation data shows a durable reversal.

tabs.gdp: Real GDP growth of 2.0% annualized is holding above contraction territory, but the composition and trajectory matter more than the headline. With consumer savings depleted to 3.6%, real purchasing power being eroded by 3.5% PCE inflation, and housing starts plateauing near 1,502K, domestic demand drivers are weakening at the margin. An oil shock of this magnitude — Brent at $113.9 — historically shaves 0.3–0.5pp from near-term GDP growth through energy cost pass-through and consumer confidence drag.
tabs.jobs: NFP at 115K MoM is a notable step down — below the ~150K threshold broadly considered consistent with stable unemployment — and suggests the labor market is absorbing tightening financial conditions with a lag. Wage growth at 3.9% YoY remains above the pace consistent with 2% inflation given trend productivity, keeping the Fed uncomfortable even as hiring slows. The combination of decelerating payrolls and still-elevated wages is a classic late-cycle labor dynamic; forward-looking indicators warrant close watch for further deterioration.
tabs.unemp: U-3 at 4.3% represents a meaningful drift higher from cycle lows and, combined with U-6 at 8.2%, reveals a 390bp spread between headline and broad unemployment — elevated underemployment and involuntary part-time work are a genuine stress signal beneath the headline. A U-6 of 8.2% indicates labor market slack is broader than U-3 suggests, which constrains consumer income resilience and spending capacity. If U-3 continues rising toward 4.5%+, recession probability models will re-price materially.
tabs.wages: Nominal wage growth of 3.9% YoY looks resilient in isolation, but against CPI at 3.3% and PCE at 3.5%, real wage gains are thin to negative depending on the deflator used. From the Fed's perspective, 3.9% wage growth remains above the ~3.0–3.5% pace consistent with 2% inflation given trend productivity, keeping services inflation sticky. A further slowdown in wages would ease the Fed's concern about a wage-price spiral but would also signal faster deterioration in consumer spending capacity.
tabs.cpi: Headline CPI jumped 49bp to 3.8% YoY — a material and alarming re-acceleration that directly contradicts the disinflation narrative the market had been pricing. Core CPI at 2.7% is more contained but Core PCE at 3.2% confirms that underlying price pressures remain well above target, giving the Fed no basis to ease. With WTI at $109.8 feeding directly into transportation and goods inflation, the risk is that headline CPI continues to drift toward 4%+, forcing the Fed to explicitly resume a tightening bias.
tabs.pce: PCE headline at 3.5% and core PCE at 3.2% are the Fed's preferred gauges and both remain significantly above the 2% mandate — this is not a close call. The 3.6% personal saving rate is a concurrent warning: consumers are spending more than their income comfortably supports, a dynamic that is unsustainable without income acceleration or a sharp pullback in consumption. The combination of below-trend savings and above-target PCE inflation points to a consumer who is increasingly price-pressured and financially fragile.
tabs.yield: The 10Y-2Y spread has steepened to 48bp with the 10Y at 4.38% and the 2Y at 3.90%, reflecting the market pricing out near-term Fed cuts as inflation re-accelerates. The 48bp positive slope is not yet a strong growth signal — it is more accurately read as a repricing of the terminal rate higher given the CPI surprise. Any further energy-driven CPI prints will push the 2Y back toward or through 4.0%, flattening the curve and increasing pressure on rate-sensitive sectors.
tabs.credit: IG OAS at 81bp and HY OAS at 282bp are historically tight relative to the macro backdrop — unemployment rising, consumer delinquencies at 2.9%, and an oil shock in progress. HY at 282bp in particular implies a default environment far more benign than late-cycle fundamentals warrant, representing a meaningful mispricing risk if growth slips below 1.5% or credit quality deteriorates in energy-sensitive sectors. A spread widening event is a higher-probability tail risk than current levels imply.
tabs.housing: At 6.37%, the 30-year mortgage rate continues to price out first-time buyers and suppress transaction volume; affordability remains severely impaired relative to any pre-2022 baseline. Housing Starts at 1,502K show builders are still active, but this supply is unlikely to clear efficiently in a demand-constrained environment where monthly payment burdens remain near historic highs. An oil-driven inflation re-acceleration risks pushing mortgage rates higher still, extending the affordability freeze and pressuring housing-related consumption.
tabs.oil: WTI surged $9.87 to $109.76 and Brent reached $118.3 — a move of this magnitude in a single snapshot period is an unambiguous supply shock signal demanding immediate reassessment of inflation forecasts. At $109+ WTI, energy's pass-through into CPI headline and PCE will be visible within 30-60 days, directly threatening the disinflationary narrative that any Fed dovish pivot depended on. This price level also acts as a demand-destruction tax on a consumer already running a 3.6% savings rate, compressing discretionary spending and widening the stagflation corridor.
tabs.banks: Rising CC delinquencies at 2.9% and a 3.6% savings rate signal deteriorating consumer credit quality, which will pressure bank provisioning and net interest income guidance in upcoming earnings. NII tailwinds from higher-for-longer rates are partially offset by increasing charge-off risk in consumer loan books, particularly in unsecured revolving credit. Banks with outsized consumer lending exposure should be monitored closely as the combination of thin savings buffers and high carry costs on variable-rate debt escalates default probability.

signal_flags.note: A 49bp single-period jump in headline CPI is a significant re-acceleration that invalidates the disinflation trajectory; materially raises the bar for any Fed easing and heightens stagflation risk.

Elevated energy prices are a primary driver of headline CPI re-acceleration and represent an uncontrolled external inflation input; further upside in crude would push headline CPI toward 4%+ within 1-2 prints.

At 160bp above the Fed's 2% target, Core PCE confirms that underlying inflation is not converging; this is the Fed's preferred gauge and its stickiness eliminates rate cut probability in the near term.

Job creation has decelerated to a level insufficient to absorb labor force growth; combined with U-6 at 8.2%, this signals a softening labor market that constrains consumer resilience as the savings buffer erodes.
A 3.6% saving rate leaves households with minimal buffer against income shocks; rising credit card delinquencies (2.9%) suggest the consumer drawdown is already translating into credit stress.
